house-robber.pattern: 1-D DP: best(i) = max(skip house i, rob it + best(i − 2))

approaches.name: Recursion: rob or skip each house
approaches.idea: For house `i`, either skip it (best of the houses before) or rob it (its money plus the best two houses back). Recurse on both choices.
steps: `best(i)` = most money from houses `0..i`; `best(−1) = best(−2) = 0`.
`best(i) = max(best(i − 1), nums[i] + best(i − 2))`.
Return `best(n − 1)`.
approaches.why: Two calls per house with the same subproblems recomputed many times.

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: Compute `dp[i]` (best for the first `i` houses) from left to right; each entry needs only the two before it.
steps: For `i` from 2 to n: `dp[i] = max(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2] + nums[i − 1])`.
Return `dp[n]`.
approaches.why: One pass with an array of n + 1 values.

approaches.name: Two rolling values
approaches.idea: Keep only `prev2` (best up to two houses back) and `prev1` (best up to the previous house).
steps: Set `prev2 = 0`, `prev1 = 0`.
For each amount `x`: `cur = max(prev1, prev2 + x)`; then `prev2 = prev1`, `prev1 = cur`.
Return `prev1`.
approaches.why: One pass with two variables.

house-robber-ii.pattern: Break the circle into two straight lines (without the first house, without the last)

approaches.name: Recursion remembering whether the first house was robbed
approaches.idea: Go house by house choosing rob or skip, carrying a flag that says whether house 0 was robbed; at the last house, robbing is allowed only if house 0 was not.
steps: `best(i, firstRobbed)`: if `i >= n`, return 0.
Skip: `best(i + 1, firstRobbed)`. Rob (if allowed — not the last house when `firstRobbed`): `nums[i] + best(i + 2, firstRobbed || i == 0)`.
Return the larger; answer `best(0, false)`.
approaches.why: Two choices per house without remembering results.

approaches.name: Two passes of House Robber
approaches.idea: The first and last houses cannot both be robbed, so the answer is the better of two straight-line problems: houses `0..n − 2` and houses `1..n − 1`. Each is the ordinary House Robber.
steps: If there is one house, return its money.
Run the two-variable House Robber on `nums[0..n − 2]` and on `nums[1..n − 1]`.
Return the larger result.
approaches.why: Two linear passes with two variables each. Every valid circular choice avoids house 0 or house n − 1, so it is counted in one of the passes.

maximum-subarray.pattern: Kadane's algorithm (best subarray ending here = max(x, previous best + x))

approaches.name: Every start, extended with a running sum
approaches.idea: Try every start and extend to the right, keeping the running sum and the best seen.
steps: For each `i`, set `sum = 0`.
For each `j >= i`, add `nums[j]` and update the best.
Return the best.
approaches.why: n(n + 1)/2 subarrays, O(1) each thanks to the running sum.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer
approaches.idea: The best subarray lies entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or crosses the middle. The crossing case is the best suffix of the left half plus the best prefix of the right half.
steps: `solve(lo, hi)`: if one element, return it.
Recursively solve both halves.
Compute the best sum ending at `mid` (going left) and the best sum starting at `mid + 1` (going right); add them.
Return the largest of the three.
approaches.why: Each level does O(n) work for the crossing sums and there are log n levels; the recursion depth is log n.

approaches.name: Kadane's algorithm
approaches.idea: The best subarray ending at `i` either extends the best one ending at `i − 1` or starts fresh at `i` — whichever is larger. A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it.
steps: Set `cur = best = nums[0]`.
For each next value `x`: `cur = max(x, cur + x)`; `best = max(best, cur)`.
Return `best`.
approaches.why: One pass with two variables. Starting from `nums[0]` (not 0) handles all-negative arrays.

maximum-product-subarray.pattern: Kadane variant tracking both the largest and the smallest product ending here

approaches.name: Every start, extended with a running product
approaches.idea: For each start, multiply in elements one by one and keep the best product seen.
steps: For each `i`, set `prod = 1`.
For each `j >= i`, multiply by `nums[j]` and update the best.
Return the best.
approaches.why: n(n + 1)/2 subarrays with O(1) work each.

approaches.name: Track the maximum and minimum product ending here
approaches.idea: A negative number turns the smallest product into the largest one. So at each position keep both the largest and the smallest product of a subarray ending there; the new values come from `x`, `max·x` and `min·x`.
steps: Set `hi = lo = best = nums[0]`.
For each next `x`: compute `a = hi·x`, `b = lo·x`; `hi = max(x, a, b)`, `lo = min(x, a, b)`.
Update `best` with `hi`; return it.
approaches.why: One pass with three variables. Taking `x` alone restarts after a zero.

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix products
approaches.idea: Within a stretch without zeros, the best product starts at the left end or ends at the right end (dropping a prefix or suffix up to an odd negative). So scan running products from both ends, restarting after zeros, and take the best value seen.
steps: Keep `left = right = 1` and `best = −∞`.
For `i` from 0 to n − 1: multiply `left` by `nums[i]` and `right` by `nums[n − 1 − i]`; update `best` with both.
If either product becomes 0, reset it to 1 (a zero splits the array) — after recording 0.
approaches.why: One pass with two products. A max-product subarray never contains a zero unless the answer is 0, and among zero-free stretches it is a prefix or a suffix.

decode-ways.pattern: 1-D DP over string positions (take one digit or two digits)

approaches.name: Recursion over the first one or two digits
approaches.idea: From position `i`, decode one digit (if it is not `0`) or two digits (if they form 10–26), and count the ways for the rest.
steps: `ways(i)`: if `i == n`, return 1 (decoded everything).
If `s[i] == "0"`, return 0 (no code starts with 0).
Return `ways(i + 1)` plus `ways(i + 2)` when `s[i..i + 1]` is between 10 and 26.
approaches.why: Up to two branches per position and no memory of results.

approaches.name: Tabulation from the end
approaches.idea: `dp[i]` = number of ways to decode `s[i..]`. Fill it from right to left with the same rule.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: if `s[i] == "0"`, `dp[i] = 0`; else `dp[i] = dp[i + 1]` plus `dp[i + 2]` if the two-digit number is ≤ 26.
Return `dp[0]`.
approaches.why: One pass over n positions with an n + 1 table.

approaches.name: Two rolling values
approaches.idea: Each `dp[i]` uses only `dp[i + 1]` and `dp[i + 2]`, so keep those two numbers.
steps: Set `next1 = 1` (dp[i + 1]) and `next2 = 0` (dp[i + 2]), starting from the end.
For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: `cur = 0` if `s[i] == "0"`, else `next1` plus `next2` when the pair is ≤ 26.
Shift: `next2 = next1`, `next1 = cur`. Return `next1`.
approaches.why: One pass with two variables.

word-break.pattern: 1-D DP over prefixes: dp[i] is true if some word ends at i after a breakable prefix

approaches.name: Recursion trying every first word
approaches.idea: From position `i`, try every dictionary word that matches at `i`; if the rest can be broken, the whole string can.
steps: `can(i)`: if `i == n`, return true.
For each word `w` with `s.startsWith(w, i)`, if `can(i + |w|)`, return true.
Return false.
approaches.why: Different word choices reach the same position many times, and each is re-explored (e.g. "aaaa…b" with words "a", "aa").

approaches.name: Memoised recursion
approaches.idea: Whether `s[i..]` can be broken depends only on `i`, so remember the answer for each position.
steps: `can(i)`: return a cached answer if there is one.
Try every word matching at `i` as before; cache and return the result.
approaches.why: n positions, each trying m words with an O(L) match check (L = word length).

approaches.name: Bottom-up DP with a word set and the longest word length
approaches.idea: `dp[i]` is true when `s[0..i)` can be broken. It is true if for some length `len` (up to the longest word), `dp[i − len]` is true and `s[i − len..i)` is a dictionary word.
steps: Put the words in a set; let `maxLen` be the longest word.
`dp[0] = true`.
For each `i` from 1 to n, for `len` from 1 to `min(i, maxLen)`: if `dp[i − len]` and the substring is in the set, set `dp[i] = true` and stop.
Return `dp[n]`.
approaches.why: n positions × up to L lengths, each building and hashing a substring of length up to L (L ≤ 20). Independent of the number of words m, which only affects the set.

longest-increasing-subsequence.pattern: O(n²) DP over "LIS ending at i", or patience sorting with binary search (O(n log n))

approaches.name: Recursion: take or skip each element
approaches.idea: Walk the array keeping the last taken value; each element can be taken (if larger) or skipped. Return the longest result.
steps: `best(i, prev)`: the longest increasing subsequence from index `i` with all values greater than `nums[prev]` (`prev = −1` means no limit).
Skip: `best(i + 1, prev)`. Take (if `prev == −1` or `nums[i] > nums[prev]`): `1 + best(i + 1, i)`.
Return the larger; answer `best(0, −1)`.
approaches.why: Every subset of positions can be explored.

approaches.name: DP: longest subsequence ending at each index
approaches.idea: `dp[i]` = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends with `nums[i]`. It is 1 plus the best `dp[j]` over earlier `j` with a smaller value.
steps: Set every `dp[i] = 1`.
For each `i`, for each `j < i` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`: `dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)`.
Return the maximum of `dp`.
approaches.why: Every pair `j < i` is checked once.

approaches.name: Patience sorting with binary search
approaches.idea: Keep `tails[k]` = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length `k + 1`. `tails` is sorted, so for each value binary search the first tail `>= x` and replace it (or append if `x` is larger than all). The length of `tails` is the answer.
steps: Start with an empty `tails`.
For each `x`: find the first index `p` with `tails[p] >= x` (lower bound).
If `p == tails.length`, append `x`; otherwise set `tails[p] = x`.
Return `tails.length`.
approaches.why: One binary search per element. Using "≥" (lower bound) makes the subsequence strictly increasing. Note `tails` is not itself an LIS — only its length is meaningful.

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.pattern: LIS DP carrying both the length and the count of subsequences ending at each index

approaches.name: Enumerate every increasing subsequence
approaches.idea: Recursively build every increasing subsequence (each element taken or skipped), tracking the longest length found and how many subsequences have it.
steps: `explore(i, prev, length)`: at the end of the array, record `length` (raise the best and reset the count, or add to the count if equal).
Always try skipping `nums[i]`; take it if it is larger than `nums[prev]`.
Return the count for the best length.
approaches.why: Every subset of positions may be visited.

approaches.name: DP with lengths and counts
approaches.idea: For each `i`, keep `len[i]` (longest increasing subsequence ending at `i`) and `cnt[i]` (how many have that length). An earlier `j` with a smaller value either gives a longer length (take over its count) or the same length (add its count).
steps: Set `len[i] = cnt[i] = 1`.
For each `j < i` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`: if `len[j] + 1 > len[i]`, set `len[i] = len[j] + 1`, `cnt[i] = cnt[j]`; else if equal, `cnt[i] += cnt[j]`.
Let `L` be the maximum length; return the sum of `cnt[i]` over all `i` with `len[i] == L`.
approaches.why: All pairs `j < i` once; two arrays of size n. (An O(n log n) version exists with a segment tree or Fenwick tree keyed by value.)

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.pattern: State-machine DP: holding, just sold (cooldown), resting

approaches.name: Recursion over each day's choice
approaches.idea: On each day you either do nothing, or buy (if not holding), or sell (if holding — and then you must skip the next day). Try every choice.
steps: `best(day, holding)`: return 0 after the last day.
Rest: `best(day + 1, holding)`.
If holding: also `prices[day] + best(day + 2, false)` (sell, skip a day). Else: also `−prices[day] + best(day + 1, true)` (buy).
Return the maximum; answer `best(0, false)`.
approaches.why: Two branches per day without memory.

approaches.name: Memoised recursion over (day, holding)
approaches.idea: The future depends only on the day and whether you hold a share: 2n states. Cache them.
steps: Same recurrence as the brute force.
Store `memo[day][holding]` and reuse it.
approaches.why: 2n states, O(1) each; the table and recursion are O(n).

approaches.name: Three rolling states
approaches.idea: At the end of each day you are in one of three states: holding a share, just sold today (cooldown tomorrow), or resting with no share. Each state's best profit depends only on yesterday's three values.
steps: Start: `hold = −∞`, `sold = 0`, `rest = 0`.
For each price `p`: `newHold = max(hold, rest − p)` (keep holding, or buy after resting); `newSold = hold + p`; `newRest = max(rest, sold)`.
Update the three values; return `max(sold, rest)`.
approaches.why: One pass with three variables. Buying only from `rest` (not from `sold`) is what enforces the cooldown.

russian-doll-envelopes.pattern: Sort by width ascending and height descending, then LIS on heights

approaches.name: Sort, then O(n²) LIS
approaches.idea: Sort envelopes by width; then nesting is an increasing chain in both width and height. `dp[i]` = longest chain ending at envelope `i`, built from every earlier envelope that is strictly smaller in both dimensions.
steps: Sort by width ascending (ties in any order).
For each `i`, `dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j])` over `j < i` with `w[j] < w[i]` and `h[j] < h[i]`.
Return the largest `dp[i]`.
approaches.why: All pairs are compared: too slow for n = 10⁵, but simple and correct.

approaches.name: Sort (width ↑, height ↓) and patience-sort the heights
approaches.idea: After sorting by width ascending, the problem is a strictly increasing subsequence of heights — except that envelopes with the same width must not chain. Sorting equal widths by height descending makes any increasing run of heights pick at most one envelope per width. Then run the O(n log n) LIS on the heights.
steps: Sort by width ascending; for equal widths, by height descending.
Run patience sorting on the heights: for each height, replace the first tail `>=` it (lower bound) or append.
Return the number of tails.
approaches.why: The sort and n binary searches are each O(n log n).

approaches.name: Try every first piece recursively
approaches.idea: Choose the first piece `j`, then either keep the rest whole or break it further; take the best product over all choices.
steps: `f(m)` = best product for a number that must be split at least once.
`f(m) = max over j in [1, m − 1] of j · max(m − j, f(m − j))`.
Return `f(n)`.
approaches.why: Without memoisation the same `f(m)` is recomputed along many paths, roughly doubling with each extra unit of n, so n = 58 is far out of reach.

approaches.name: Bottom-up DP
approaches.idea: Compute the best product for every value up to n, reusing smaller answers.
steps: For `i` from 2 to `n`: `best[i] = max over j in [1, i − 1] of max(j, best[j]) · max(i − j, best[i − j])`.
Return `best[n]`, where `n` itself must be split, so the loop for `n` never leaves it whole.
approaches.why: n values, each trying up to n split points. `max(x, best[x])` lets a part stay whole (for parts, not splitting is allowed); `best[n]` is built only from genuine splits.

approaches.name: As many 3s as possible
approaches.idea: Any piece of 5 or more is better split (2 · (k − 2) > k), 4 = 2 + 2 changes nothing, and three 2s are worse than two 3s. So the best split uses 3s, plus one 2 or one 4 at the end.
steps: If `n <= 3`, return `n − 1` (the split is forced: 1 + 1 or 1 + 2).
While `n > 4`, multiply the product by 3 and subtract 3 from `n`.
Multiply by what is left (2, 3 or 4) and return.
approaches.why: The loop runs n / 3 times; using fast exponentiation on 3 would make it O(log n). Stopping at 4 avoids leaving a 1 (3 + 1 is worse than 2 + 2). The answer for n = 58 is 3¹⁸ · 4, which still fits in an int.

maximum-sum-circular-subarray.pattern: Kadane for the maximum and the minimum (wrap = total − min)

approaches.name: Every start, every length
approaches.idea: For each start index, extend the subarray one element at a time around the circle (up to n elements) and track the best running sum.
steps: For each `start`, set `sum = 0`.
For `len` from 1 to `n`, add `nums[(start + len − 1) % n]` to `sum` and update the best.
Return the best.
approaches.why: n starts times n lengths: about 9 · 10⁸ steps at n = 3 · 10⁴, which times out on the large test.

approaches.name: Kadane + best prefix and suffix
approaches.idea: A wrapping subarray is a suffix plus a prefix that do not overlap. Precompute the best prefix sum ending at or before each index, then combine it with every suffix.
steps: Run Kadane for the best non-wrapping sum.
Build `bestPrefix[i]` = the largest prefix sum using `nums[0..i]`.
For each split, combine the suffix sum `nums[i..n − 1]` with `bestPrefix[i − 1]`, and return the overall maximum.
approaches.why: Linear time, and easy to reason about, but it needs an extra array. The total − minimum trick below gets the same answer with O(1) memory.

approaches.name: max(Kadane max, total − Kadane min)
approaches.idea: A wrapping subarray leaves out one contiguous middle block, so its sum is `total − middle`. The best wrap removes the minimum-sum subarray. Track the maximum and minimum subarray sums in the same pass.
steps: In one pass, maintain Kadane's running maximum and running minimum, plus the total.
If the best maximum is negative (all numbers negative), return it.
Otherwise return `max(best, total − worst)`.
approaches.why: When every number is negative, the minimum subarray is the whole array, and `total − worst = 0` would describe an empty subarray, which is not allowed. That guard is the classic trap.

longest-turbulent-subarray.pattern: DP on the last comparison (up / down run lengths)

approaches.name: Extend from every start
approaches.idea: From each start index, extend to the right while the comparison sign keeps flipping, and record the longest run.
steps: For each `i`, set `len = 1` and walk `j = i + 1, i + 2, …`.
Stop at an equal pair, or when the sign of `arr[j] − arr[j − 1]` does not flip relative to the previous step.
Track the maximum `len`.
approaches.why: On a fully turbulent array every start extends to the end, giving about n² / 2 = 8 · 10⁸ steps for n = 4 · 10⁴, so it times out on the large test.

approaches.name: Up and down run lengths
approaches.idea: Keep two numbers: the longest turbulent subarray ending here whose last step went up, and the one whose last step went down. Each new step extends the opposite one.
steps: Start with `up = down = best = 1`.
If `arr[i] > arr[i − 1]`: `up = down + 1`, `down = 1`. If smaller: `down = up + 1`, `up = 1`. If equal: both become 1.
Update `best` with the larger of the two after each step.
approaches.why: A step up can only follow a step down in a turbulent run, so the new up-length is the old down-length + 1. This is a two-state DP, the same idea as "wiggle subsequence" but for contiguous runs. A sliding window over sign changes is an equivalent view.

stone-game-iii.pattern: Game DP on score difference (minimax as max of negatives)

approaches.name: Recursive minimax
approaches.idea: Let `diff(i)` be the best score difference (player to move minus opponent) from stone `i` on. Try taking 1, 2 or 3 stones and subtract the opponent's best difference afterwards.
steps: `diff(n) = 0`.
`diff(i) = max over k in 1..3 (with i + k <= n) of (sum of stones i..i + k − 1) − diff(i + k)`.
Compare `diff(0)` with 0 to name the winner.
approaches.why: Each call branches three ways and nothing is cached, so it is exponential and only survives tiny inputs.

approaches.name: Bottom-up difference DP
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[i]` from the end of the row backwards. Each entry depends only on the next three, so every position is solved once.
steps: Set `dp[n] = 0` (and treat positions past the end as unavailable).
For `i` from `n − 1` down to 0: `dp[i] = max over k = 1..3 of (stones i..i + k − 1) − dp[i + k]`.
Return "Alice" if `dp[0] > 0`, "Bob" if `< 0`, otherwise "Tie".
approaches.why: Three choices per position. Storing the difference instead of both scores turns a two-player game into one maximisation: the opponent's best outcome is subtracted. Only dp[i + 1..i + 3] are read, so four rolling variables would make it O(1) space.
